title: Datathon: Hands-on Afternoon Activity
text:
Island Fox (Urocyon littoralis)
The island fox is a small, charismatic canid species endemic to six of the eight Channel Islands off the coast of southern California. It’s one of the best examples of island dwarfism, having evolved from the mainland gray fox (Urocyon cinereoargenteus) to become significantly smaller.
In the 1990s, several island fox populations faced near extinction due to golden eagle predation, canine distemper virus, and habitat degradation. The island fox was listed as endangered in 2004. Recovery efforts of the island fox included removal of golden eagles, vaccination and captive breeding programs, reintroduction of native bald eagles, and habitat restoration.

title: Datathon: Hands-on Afternoon Activity
text:
Mini Datathon
First, please go through the Introduction which includes data preparation and some basics of how this dataset looks like. Then start with Part I which has a collection of analysis questions for you to work through. Depending on your level of comfort, take also a look at Part II which has some more Advanced challenges. If you’re ambitious, you can do both, or even come up with your own questions. There are definitely more challenges listed than what is feasible to do in 90 minutes, so tackle those that are of most interest to you. Remember that data science is always about combining numbers/tables and figures into a story. Coding and statistics are just tools to get there. So for instance, if you’re fascinated about how/why foxes are being vaccinated, it’s totally ok to google for additional background.
We have an Optional Share-Out during the last portion of the Datathon: participants can present one result of their choosing to the group. If you would like to do so, make sure to invest time in making a nice plot: play around with the plot theme, font sizes, color palettes, labels and layout. Google (via its automatic Gemini search results) is a good tool to dive deep into the myriad ggplot customization options. Note that everything in the plot can be customized to your choosing, which is (one of) the power of using a statistical package.
If you are stuck at any point of the Datathon, raise your hand and a Data Guide will help you out

Data and Prep
The data provided is part of an ongoing longitudinal study of island foxes from 2014 to 2016 of trap monitoring. This resulted in collection of 4,975 recorded trap observations, which may have contained a fox or not. Other information collected were Sex, Age Class, Weight, Body Condition, Reproductive Status, and Vaccinations. Information on the data collected can be found in the Databook.

Cleaning Data

Renaming Categories
Looking at the Codebook, the variables Vaccinations, ReproductiveStatus and BodyCondition are coded in interesting ways. In Vaccinations, missing values (NA) are considered as not vaccinated; therefore, changing the missing to “NV” will ensure that they are correctly classified. In ReproductiveStatus, the missing values (NA) indicate unknown reproductive status. In BodyCondition, the numerical values 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, represent a condition. To make the condition easier, we will convert them to the categories. Run the code below to alter them:

df <- df |> mutate( # Will change the variables in the df data set
    Vaccinations = case_when(is.na(Vaccinations) ~ "NV", .default = Vaccinations), # Reclassifies Missing Data in Vaccination as "N" per code book.
    ReproductiveStatus = case_when(is.na(ReproductiveStatus) ~ "UN", .default = ReproductiveStatus), # Reclassifies Missing Data in Vaccination as "N" per code book.
    BodyCondition = case_when( # Begins to modify BodyCondition
        as.character(BodyCondition) == "1" ~ "emaciated", # Changes 1 to emaciated
        as.character(BodyCondition) == "2" ~ "thin", # Changes 2 to thin
        as.character(BodyCondition) == "3" ~ "healthy wild", # Changes 3 to healthy wild 
        as.character(BodyCondition) == "4" ~ "extra fat reserves", # Changes 4 to Extra Fat Reserve
        as.character(BodyCondition) == "5" ~ "extreme fat reserves" # Changes 5 to Extreme Fat Reserves
        )
    )

title: Datathon: Hands-on Afternoon Activity
text:
Part I:

Fox Weight Analysis
Imagine you’re a field biologist tracking animal health across the remote Santa Rosa and San Miguel Islands. You’ve noticed that some animals seem heavier in certain years—but is it just your imagination, or is there a real trend?
The Weght variable contains information of the Fox’s weight in kilograms. Let’s start by calculating the mean weight and standard deviation of weight using mean() and sd() functions:

mean_weight<-mean(df$Weight)
sd_weight<-sd(df$Weight)
mean_weight

[1] 1.940275

sd_weight #printing the values

[1] 0.4140872


We see that mean weight of a fox is about 1.9 kg (which is about 4 pounds) with standard deviation about .41 kg.
We use the table() and prop.table() functions to get the frequencies and proportions for the Sex.

count_df <- table(df$Sex) # Using the 'Sex' variable from the `df` data set, we count the frequencies of each category with the table function and storing it in rs_df.
count_df # Printing out the contents of "rs_df"


Female   Male 
   923   1044 


Using the table() function, we can see that there were 923 female and 1044 male Foxes captured.

prop.table(count_df) # Computing the Proportions of "rs_df"


   Female      Male 
0.4692425 0.5307575 


The prop.table() function shows the respective percentages: there are slightly more male Foxes (about 53%) vs. female Foxes (about 47%).
We can visualize the data using the ggplot functions. Namely we build a bar plot that shows those above counts visually (with more Male than Female foxes):

ggplot(df) + # Setting up the data to create a plot.
  geom_bar(aes(Sex)) + # Creating a bar chart based on the variable "ReproductiveStatus" 
  theme(axis.title = element_text(size = 14), axis.text = element_text(size = 14))










Weight vs Sex
Let’s visualize the variable Weight and Sex with a boxplot using ggplot:

ggplot(df, aes(x = Sex, y = Weight)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Boxplot of Weight by Sex",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Weight"
  ) + theme_minimal()








From the box plot we see that male Foxs tend to be slightly heavier than female Foxes.
We can use group_by() function to separate male from female population and calculate means and standard deviations separately:

weight_summary <- df %>%
  group_by(Sex) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_weight = mean(Weight),
    sd_weight = sd(Weight),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
weight_summary

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  Sex    mean_weight sd_weight
  <chr>        <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Female        1.88     0.386
2 Male          1.99     0.431


This table confirms that male Foxes are slightly heavier, with mean weight of about 1.99 kg, than female Foxes, whose mean weight is about 1.88 kg. Standard deviations are also slightly higher for male Foxes.

Weight vs Sex over time
To see weight vs sex trend over time we can use group_by() and ggplot functions again:

weight_summary_yearly <- df %>%
  group_by(Sex, SamplingYear) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_weight = mean(Weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_weight = sd(Weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) #group the data by Sex and Year and calculate mean and standard deviation of weight
weight_summary_yearly

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  Sex    SamplingYear mean_weight sd_weight
  <chr>         <dbl>       <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Female         2014        1.95     0.362
2 Female         2015        1.85     0.409
3 Female         2016        1.86     0.373
4 Male           2014        2.08     0.405
5 Male           2015        1.95     0.451
6 Male           2016        1.99     0.419


From the table we see a downward trend in weight for both females and males across years. Let’s plot it on the graph:

ggplot(weight_summary_yearly, aes(x = SamplingYear, y = mean_weight)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_weight - sd_weight,
                    ymax = mean_weight + sd_weight), width = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ Sex) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Weight by Year and Sex",
    y = "Mean Weight",
    x = "Year"
  )














Weight vs Sex over time by Island



Here is a first question for you to answer: do the foxes on different islands have the same weight? Is there an island where the foxes are significantly heavier than others? To conduct such analysis, you can filter by different Islands:

#Santa Rosa Fox population 

SR_df<-filter(df,Island=="SRI")

#San Miguel Fox population
SM_df<-filter(df,Island=="SMI")






Questions to Try Out






Vaccinations



Do vaccinated foxes have a different weight compared to unvaccinated ones? To answer this, study the relationship between Weight and Vaccinations








Body Condition



The dataset has a variable called BodyCondition. What proportion of foxes are well nourished? Do some islands have a larger proportion of “fat” foxes than others? How does BodyCondition connect with Weight? For the latter, you could look into scatter plots.




Fox Reproductive Status Analysis
The ReproductiveStatus variable contains information of the Fox’s reproductive status when captures. This data is recorded as “N” (Not actively reproductive), “L” (Lactating), “SL” (Signs of Lactating), and “TD” (Testes Distended).
We will use the table() and prop.table() function to get the frequencies and proportions for the ReproductiveStatus.

rs_df <- table(df$ReproductiveStatus) # Using the 'ReproductiveStatus' variable from the `df` data set, we count the frequencies of each category with the table function and storing it in rs_df.
rs_df # Printing out the contents of "rs_df"


   L   SL   TD   UN 
  18  244 1030  675 


Using the table() function, we can see that there are 3 common reproductive statuses by Fox: “L” at 18, “SL” at 244, “TD” at 1030, and “UN” at 675.

prop.table(rs_df) # Computing the Proportions of "rs_df"


          L          SL          TD          UN 
0.009150991 0.124046772 0.523640061 0.343162176 


Using the prop.table() function, we can see that that the most common status is “TD” at 52.4% and the least common is “L” at the 0.9%. Both “SL” and “UN” represent 12.4% and 34.3% of the data, respectively. In barplot format we have:

ggplot(df) + # Setting up the data to create a plot.
  geom_bar(aes(ReproductiveStatus)) # Creating a bar chart based on the variable "ReproductiveStatus"









Sex and Reproductive Status
Let’s compare the frequencies between the variables Sex and Reproductive Status. We will be using the same table() function:

xy_df <- table(df$ReproductiveStatus, df$Sex)
# Use the variables "ReproductiveStatus" and "Sex" from the "df" data set
# Use the table function to compute the crosstabs
# Store the results in the xy_df object

xy_df # Print results out

    
     Female Male
  L      18    0
  SL    244    0
  TD      0 1030
  UN    661   14


The results show that certain categorical combinations between ReproductiveStatus and Sex are 0, which is to be expected. The category “UN” is found in both Male and Female foxes. Looking at Female foxes, The most common type is “UN”, followed by “SL”. For Male foxes, the most common type was “TD”.
Let’s find the proportions for each the combination of the variables using the prop.table() function.

prop.table(xy_df)

    
          Female        Male
  L  0.009150991 0.000000000
  SL 0.124046772 0.000000000
  TD 0.000000000 0.523640061
  UN 0.336044738 0.007117438


We can see that 52.4% of the data are Male and “TD” foxes, 33.6% of the data are Female and “UN” foxes, and 12.4% of the data are Female and “SL” foxes. To visualize how the variable ReproductiveStatus and Sex related to each other we use a stacked bar plot:

ggplot(df) +
  geom_bar(aes(Sex, fill = ReproductiveStatus)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.title = element_text(size = 14), axis.text = element_text(size = 14))








The plot indicate which categories are most dominant in each sex. We can see that the most dominant reproductive status in Male foxes is testes distended. For Female foxes, we can see that the most common reproductive status is Unknown.



Challenges
The list below is quite long: pick and choose the challenges that appeal to you the most.






Age Class



How does ReproductiveStatus relate to AgeClass (how old is the fox), to Vaccinations, and to Capture Type?








Skunking



How many skunks were caught each year? Are there more skunks on some island than others? (Look at TrapResult. Note that some skunks were caught but escaped, see the different possible values of this field!)








Fox Ages



What is the Age distribution of the foxes? How many foxes are less than 1 year old? Does this vary by year or by island? (Look at AgeClass. Notice that it’s a numeric variable)








Trap Effectiveness



Analyze how often do the traps work (expressed as a success percentage). Namely, which Island and which Years yield the most foxes?








Record Foxes



A fun exercise is to analyze the extreme fox records. What was the fattest fox ever caught (break this out by Year, by Sex, and by Island)? What is the latest date of a fox capture in this dataset? What is the oldest fox?

Looking at these records, we can see that it is a Female fox on Santa Rosa Island that was observed 3 times during the same week in August 2016. The first capture it was tagged (CaptureType = New) and then it was re-tagged twice more.


Questions to Try Out






Tagging Statistics



How many different foxes have been tagged? If you look at `CaptureType’ you can also analyze how many foxes have been observed multiple times. What fraction of foxes were observed just once? How many unique foxes are on each of the two islands?








Fox Life Story



Find an ``interesting’’ fox that has been observed across a lengthy interval of time (multiple months and years). Investigate its record and write down a story about the life of this fox. For example: how did its weight, reproductive and vaccination status evolve over time? The aim of this Challenge is to convert the data/numbers into a verbal narrative/words.



Time Series
While above we considered the general population trends of how foxes are across the years, this evidence is not so conclusive because potentially it is about different foxes. A stronger analysis would directly track the same fox across time. Time series, where we put the date (in our case TrapDate) on the x-axis and the numeric variable of interest (say Weight) on the y-axis serve this purpose. To be interesting however, the time span needs to be long enough – it is not so interesting to make a time series for fox 989001000124022 that was only ever observed over a single week in 2016.
We can use the piping mechanism to simultaneously filter a specific fox and analyze its record. For instance below, we create a bar plot showing when a given fox was captured: 3 times in 2014 and twice in 2015:

df |> filter(Pittag==989001000415721) |>    # filter by pit tag
  ggplot() + geom_bar(aes(factor(SamplingYear))) # then plot only those rows














Fox Time Series



Find foxes that are observed across multiple months/years and create time series plots for them. Report how your findings align or differ from the population-analysis we did in the Introduction.

title: Welcome to Santa Barbara Data Day!
text:
In this introductory one-hour workshop we will learn the basics of R for working with tabular data (think of a spreadsheet, with rows and columns) and plotting.
Our goals for this first session are:

title: Welcome to Santa Barbara Data Day!
text:
What are R and RStudio?
We are working with two pieces of software (or apps) at the same time: R and RStudio.

R refers to a programming language as well as the software that runs R code.

For example, I could type 2+2 in the Console, and that’s purely R. It interprets my input and makes the necessary calculations.

RStudio is a software interface that can make it easier to write R scripts and interact with the R software.

It is called an Integrated Development Environment (IDE), where we can see other relevant stuff for our data analysis with R.

title: Welcome to Santa Barbara Data Day!
text:
The RStudio layout
Let’s create a new script to start exploring RStudio. On the top menu, click ‘File’ > ‘New File’ > ‘R Script’.



RStudio screenshot. Source: datacarpentry.org


In the above screenshot, we can see 4 “panes” in the default layout:

Top-Left: the Source pane that displays scripts and files open.
Top-Right: the Environment pane, which shows all the objects in your current R session (Environment).

There’s other tabs there, but we’ll focus only on the Environment tab.

Bottom-Left: the Console pane, where you can interact directly with an R console, which interprets R commands and prints the results.

There are also tabs for Terminal and Jobs. Again, we will focus only on the Console tab.

Bottom-Right: the Files/Plots/Help/Viewer pane to navigate files or view plots and help pages.

title: Welcome to Santa Barbara Data Day!
text:
Console vs R script
Working in R offers two primary methods: the Console and Scripts. Think of it like cooking a meal.

The Console (winging it): It is for quick, immediate execution of commands. Like improvising a dish without a recipe, you get results fast, but you can’t easily replicate the process later.
R Scripts (the saved recipe): A script is a text file where you record your code. Like a well-documented recipe, it ensures your work is repeatable and shareable. It’ has several pros:

Reproducibility: You can re-run the entire “recipe” with one click months later.
Editing: Easily tweak steps without starting over.
Comments: Use the # symbol to write notes. R ignores these lines, making them perfect for explaining why you wrote a specific piece of code.

title: Welcome to Santa Barbara Data Day!
text:
Running code from a script
Let’s type some code in our script, for example

(2 * 5) / 4

[1] 2.5


There are multiple ways to run this code:

You can place your cursor in any part of the line of code and click the ‘Run’ button at the top-right corner of the script pane.
Or even better, you can use a keyboard shortcut, Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter if you’re using a Mac) to run the line of code.

Important:

White space (empty lines) does not affect code. It is encouraged to make code more readable
In the console you’ll see the > prompt when R is ready to receive a new command. If it is waiting for more instructions from you, you will see + sign. For example, try running the following code


(2 ** 3) -

You can see the + sign telling you R is waiting for further instruction. This will happen for example when you forget to close a parenthesis. The easiest way to fix it is pressing the Esc key, fixing the code in your script, and running it again.

title: Welcome to Santa Barbara Data Day!
text:
Creating objects
Most of the time we will be creating objects in our R environment that we can later call, reuse, and modify.
For example, to create an object called age with the number value of my current age, I would type

age <- 30

I will see this variable show up in my Environment pane.
If I want to calculate how old I will be in 50 years, I can type

age + 50

[1] 80


If you want to create a new object called future_age with this value, you can run

future_age <- age + 50

Important:

R is case sensitive, so take that into consideration when typing commands and object names
Take advantage of RStudio autocompletion! After typing a few characters, use the Tab key
Don’t use whitespaces in your variable names (don’t create my name <-, but my_name <- instead), and don’t start them with numbers.

title: Welcome to Santa Barbara Data Day!
text:
Functions
When programming, it is usual to call functions to perform a given task. Functions take inputs (also called arguments), perform the task with those inputs, and (oftentimes) return an output.
To start working today with some real data, let’s call the R built-in function data to load the Palmer penguins dataset

data("penguins")

We can take a look at our dataset clicking it in the Environment pane, or using the View function.



Palmer penguins. Source: allisonhorst.github.io

title: Welcome to Santa Barbara Data Day!
text:
Libraries
With a huge community of open-source developers around R, its capabilities are being expanded every day. Third-party libraries bring additional functions to R, and we can install them using the install.packages('library_name') command.
Today, we will only use the tidyverse library, which brings with it a number of other libraries, but there’s only the need to install and load the tidyverse library.

install.packages('tidyverse')

After installing it, we can load it into our current R environment

Remember:

We only need to install a given library with install.packages() once in our computer.
We need to load the library with library() once per R session, basically every time we open RStudio. Add it in all your scripts for reproducibility.

title: Welcome to Santa Barbara Data Day!
text:
Challenge: Removing missing values
With what you already know (about creating new objects, functions, and arguments), use the drop_na() function to create a new object called penguins_clean, using as an argument our penguins object. When finished, see the documentation for this function running the ?drop_na() command.

# Solution
penguins_clean <- drop_na(penguins)

title: Welcome to Santa Barbara Data Day!
text:
Our first scatter plot
We use the ggplot() function to create a plot. In order to tell it what data to use, we need to specify the data argument.

ggplot(data = penguins_clean)








We get a blank plot because we haven’t told ggplot() which variables we want to correspond to parts of the plot. We can specify the “mapping” of variables to plot elements, such as x/y coordinates, size, or shape, by using the aes() function.

# adding a mapping to x and y axes
ggplot(data = penguins_clean, mapping = aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass))








Now we’ve got a plot with x and y axes corresponding to variables from penguins_clean. However, we haven’t specified how we want the data to be displayed. We do this using geom_ functions, which specify the type of geometry we want, such as points, lines, or bars. We can add a geom_point() layer to our plot by using the + sign. We indent onto a new line to make it easier to read.

ggplot(data = penguins_clean, mapping = aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass)) +
  geom_point()








As you can see, geom_point() created a scatter plot. Each point represents an observation, a penguin, and its location on the plot shows that penguin’s flipper length and body mass. As expected, the plot clearly shows a trend: penguins with longer flippers usually weigh more.
Do you think there’s an additional relationship of these two variables with the species of the penguins? We can add a third variable using the color argument inside the aes() function.

ggplot(data = penguins_clean, mapping = aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, color = species)) +
  geom_point()








To know all the things we can do with ggplot, check the following resources:

ggplot cheatsheet. You can also have access to it inside RStudio, from the menu Help > Cheat Sheets > Data Visualization with ggplot2
The R Graph Gallery
from Data to Viz

title: Welcome to Santa Barbara Data Day!
section: Challenge: Changing the shape of points
text:
Challenge: Changing the shape of points
To make our previous plot even easier to read, let’s make each species have a different shape in the plot. For this, use the shape argument inside the aes() function.

# Solution
ggplot(data = penguins_clean, mapping = aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, color = species, shape = species)) +
  geom_point()

title: Welcome to Santa Barbara Data Day!
text:
Using bar plots
All ggplots will follow the structure we just used: call ggplot(), specify the mapping of variables with aes(), and the plot type we want with a given geom_*().
Let’s do now a bar plot, counting the number of penguins in each island. This is straightforward, using geom_bar as our geometry.

ggplot(data = penguins_clean, mapping = aes(x = island)) +
  geom_bar()








To give a more professional look to our plot, we can modify the axis labels and add a title using the labs() function, like this:

ggplot(data = penguins_clean, mapping = aes(x = island)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Number of penguins per island",
       x = "Island",
       y = "Count")

title: Welcome to Santa Barbara Data Day!
text:
Challenge: Make your own plot
Using the penguins dataset, make your own plot. Look at the cheatsheet or the Graph Gallery for inspiration. To give you a couple of ideas, try a histogram or a box plot. Or add another variable to our previous scatter and bar plots.
If you are up for a harder challenge, look into faceting, here is an example:

ggplot(penguins_clean, aes(x = flipper_len, y = body_mass, color = species)) +
  geom_point() + 
  facet_wrap(~island) +
  labs(title = "Size vs Weight Across Different Islands",
       x = "Flipper Length (mm)",
       y = "Body Mass (g)",
       color = "Species")

What is Markdown?
Markdown is a way to write a document using plain text. You can open a Markdown file on any computer, without needing a specialized application or the internet, unlike Google Docs, Microsoft Word, or PDFs.
It uses specific syntax (special characters) to add styling to text instead of making you click formatting buttons in an application toolbar.
Basic Markdown Syntax
Here is how you format text in Markdown:
Headers:
# Biggest Header

## Second Biggest Header

### Third Biggest Header
Text Styles:
*This text will be italicized* **This text will be bold**
Lists:
-   Item 1
-   Item 2
    -   Sub-item A

title: Welcome to Santa Barbara Data Day!
text:
What is Quarto?
Quarto is the engine that takes your Markdown file and “renders” it. It runs the R code, creates the graphs, and weaves everything into a beautiful final document (like this HTML page, a PDF, or even a presentation).
This is a core skill in Reproducible Research: If your data changes tomorrow, you just click Render, and your entire report updates automatically!
